introduction: On this first Sunday of Lent, Moses teaches the people to remember how God brought them out of slavery and to offer him their first fruits. In the Gospel, Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, is tempted in the desert for forty days and answers the devil with the word of God. Paul tells us that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. Let us begin our Lenten journey with Jesus.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord is near to all who call on him. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that this Lent may be a time of conversion and renewal for all her members. Let us pray to the Lord.
For catechumens preparing for Baptism at Easter: that they may be strengthened against every temptation. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are tempted, discouraged or tired: that they may find strength in God's word. Let us pray to the Lord.
For refugees and migrants, who remember a hard journey like Israel's: that they may find welcome and a home. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that our prayer, fasting and almsgiving may draw us closer to God and to our neighbor. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, your Son was led by the Spirit into the desert and overcame temptation. Strengthen us this Lent with your word, and bring us to the joy of Easter. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Led by the Spirit into the desert
reflection.body:
The first reading gives us an ancient prayer of thanksgiving. When the Israelites bring the first fruits of their harvest, they recite their history: "My father was a Syrian ready to perish." They remember slavery in Egypt, their cry to God, and how "The LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand." Then they offer the first of everything to the God who gave them freedom. Lent begins with remembering what God has done for us.

In the Gospel, Jesus, "full of the Holy Spirit," is "led by the Spirit into the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil." Luke describes three temptations. Each one is a shortcut: to use his power for himself (turning stone into bread), to gain the kingdoms of the world by worshiping the devil, and to force God to prove his care by throwing himself from the temple.

Jesus answers each temptation with the word of God. "Man shall not live by bread alone." "You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only." "You shall not tempt the Lord your God." He does not argue with the devil; he holds on to God.

Luke adds a sober note at the end: the devil "departed from him until another time." Temptation does not disappear after one victory. But Jesus has shown us how to resist.

Paul tells us that faith is near: "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart." And he gives a promise for every struggle: "Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved."

This Lent, choose a short verse of Scripture to hold on to when temptation comes. Make a simple plan for prayer, fasting and giving. And call on the name of the Lord often.
